material: screenprint
subject_matter: Ludwig van Beethoven, sheet music, portrait, vivid color, graphic contrasts, cultural icon, writing, 20th century, vibrant background, artistic interpretation
description_block:
Beethoven forms part of the final body of screenprints created by Andy Warhol in 1987, shortly before his untimely death. Drawing upon Joseph Karl Stieler's celebrated 1820 portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven, Warhol reimagined the composer through his characteristic use of vivid colour and bold graphic contrasts. In doing so, he recast Beethoven as a twentieth-century cultural icon, placing him alongside the celebrities, artists and public figures that populated his oeuvre.
Throughout his career, Warhol explored the mechanisms through which individuals become cultural icons. Whereas his portraits of Marilyn Monroe, Elvis Presley and Elizabeth Taylor examined the phenomenon of twentieth-century celebrity, Beethoven applies the same lens to a figure whose legacy transcends time and geography. Striking colour contrasts and graphic intervention reinvigorate the nineteenth-century portrait, highlighting the enduring power of Beethoven's image in the modern imagination.
The present work is a trial proof in a unique colourway, produced during the printmaking process to evaluate possible colour palettes, registration and overall visual impact prior to the finalisation of the edition. Such impressions offer valuable insight into the artist's working methods and the close collaboration between Warhol and his master printers. Created at the culmination of his career, Beethoven encapsulates Warhol's enduring engagement with celebrity, the power of repetition and cultural mythology. By translating one of Western music's most celebrated figures into the visual language of Pop Art, he created an image that bridges historical tradition and contemporary culture with remarkable immediacy.

material: screenprints
subject_matter: dancers, movement, costumes, portraits, performance, emotion, expression, theatricality, choreography, color
description_block:
Created in 1986, Andy Warhol's Martha Graham portfolio pays tribute to one of the most influential and transformative figures in twentieth-century dance. Widely regarded as the founder of modern dance, Graham rejected the conventions of classical ballet in favour of a highly expressive movements that emphasised emotion, psychological depth and the physical capabilities of the body. Her revolutionary approach reshaped the landscape of contemporary performance and established a legacy that continues to influence dancers and choreographers worldwide.
Rather than depicting Graham through a single likeness, Warhol selected a series of celebrated photographs capturing her in some of her most renowned roles. These images, originally intended to document fleeting live performances, are reimagined through vibrant colour and dramatic contrasts. In Warhol's hands, Graham's theatrical gestures and commanding stage presence acquire a renewed visual intensity, preserving the dynamism of her performances.
The portfolio reflects an important aspect of Warhol's late career, when his portraiture increasingly expanded beyond film stars and popular entertainers to encompass individuals whose achievements had fundamentally shaped cultural history. Graham's inclusion within his body of work acknowledges her significance not only as a performer, but also as a pioneering creative force whose influence extended far beyond the stage.
Produced just one year before the artist's death, the Martha Graham portfolio demonstrates Warhol's continued mastery of portraiture and his enduring interest in the ways images preserve and disseminate cultural legacy. By transforming archival photographs into bold and compelling screenprints, he paid homage to another artist whose innovations altered the course of their field.

description_block: Study of 'The Entrance', from My Normandy belongs to the celebrated body of work inspired by David Hockney's bucolic home in rural Normandy, where he captured the ever-changing light of his own picturesque garden and the surrounding environs. description_block: Separation II emerged from Munch's early exploration of transfer lithography and demonstrates his desire to experiment with unconventional techniques. Instead of drawing directly onto a lithographic stone or a prepared transfer sheet, Munch worked on a sheet of paper laid over a coarse textile surface. As he drew with crayon, the irregular weave of the fabric was impressed into the image, creating a distinctive texture. When subsequently transferred to stone and printed, this process produced the remarkable sense of depth, atmosphere and translucency evident in the present impression. This impression was most likely produced by Lassally in Berlin, as several comparable impressions printed in deep blue on thin Japan paper bear Lassally's signature, dated 1906-9.

description_block: MaternitÃ© is one of five rare, experimental hectographs produced by Picasso in 1938. A precursor to the modern photocopying processes, hectography involved transferring an image, executed with specially formulated ink, onto a gelatin matrix from which successive impressions could be taken. Although the technique was capable of yielding multiple examples, typically between twenty and one hundred impressions before the deterioration of the image, only a very limited number of examples from Picasso's brief engagement with the medium are known today, making these works exceptionally scarce.
